definition: Reporting a result within bands of instance difficulty rather than over an aggregate, and across 4 sources the analysis that turns a benchmark number into a mechanism claim. Its clearest use: a verifier-free selector is neutral or fractionally worse on the easy tier (99.9 against 99.9, 99.1 against 100.0) while moving the medium tier 58.1 to 70.3 and 74.9 to 88.6 and the hard tier 3.7 to 8.1 and 13.4 to 17.2 -- the pattern a mechanism-driven improvement should show and one the aggregate conceals. A second source stratifies abstention rather than accuracy and finds refusal rates rising monotonically with difficulty, 2.1 percent on two-step problems against 14.8 on problems needing five or more, which is its evidence against a uniform refusal strategy. The standing caveats both sources acknowledge: benchmark difficulty is an approximate proxy for what a particular policy can answer, and tiers defined by a baseline's own pass rate select for that baseline's failures, so part of any lift is regression toward the mean. The archive's related finding is that this decomposition is cheap and its absence is a choice, since an aggregate can move opposite to most of its components.

evidence.note: Separates hallucination into a reasoning failure and a knowledge failure, treats the first with a structured reflect-before-answering format and the second with a reward for abstaining when no sampled chain succeeds, and shows the two mechanisms are not interchangeable -- reflection alone never abstains, abstention alone never lowers the hallucination proxy.
evidence.title: REIN: Bridging the Gap between Reasoning and Reliability via Reflection and Abstention Alignment

evidence.note: Replaces GRPO's z-score group normalisation with a temperature-scaled softmax over rewards, which keeps the induced prompt-difficulty weighting bounded as pass probability approaches one and turns the temperature into a dial between REINFORCE and maximum-likelihood weighting.
evidence.title: SoftmaxGRPO: Learning to Reason using Softmax Advantage Group Estimation

evidence.note: Shows that selecting the most confident rollout can be worse than picking at random, because uniformly high confidence signals a failure to explore rather than a well-supported answer, and replaces maximisation with a temporal criterion that penalises early certainty while requiring late certainty.
evidence.title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling

evidence.note: Measures, under a pre-registered confirmatory design, how often majority-vote self-consistency lowers per-problem accuracy on a hard science benchmark, and shows that two cheap verifier-free gates recover essentially none of the headroom a per-problem oracle marks out.
evidence.title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs

name: difficulty stratification
